MINUTES OF THE MORNING SESSION
THURSDAY, JUNE 26, 1947
Washington Athletic Club
Seattle, Washington
THE
annual Convention, held in the 114th year of the Psi Upsilon
Fraternity and with the Theta Theta Chapter as host, was called to
order at 10 :00 A.M. at the Washington Athletic Club. Seattle. Washington.
by Earle W. Zinn, Theta Theta '36, Chairman of the Alumni Convention
Committee.
Brother Zinn introduced James Piper, Theta Theta '46, who, as Presi
dent of the Theta Theta Chapter, brought the greetings of the Chapter to
the Convention, and Frank I. White, Theta Theta '18, who extended greet
ings as President of the Psi Upsilon Alumni Association of the State of
Washington. Dean David Thomson. Theta Theta '92. Vice-President
Emeritus of the University of Washington, was introduced by Brother
Zinn, and Brother Thomson introduced Dr. Raymond T. Allen, President
of the University of Washington, who addressed the Convention and
extended the greetings and good wishes of the University of Washington.
LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01, President of The Executive Council, was
then introduced by Brother Zinn. Brother Weed welcomed the delegates
and expressed the apprecation of the delegates for the warm hospitality
already extended by the alumni and undergraduate Brothers of the Theta
Theta Chapter.
On motion, duly adopted, LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01, was elected
Temporary President of the Convention. Brother Weed appointed Edward
T. Richards, Sigma '27, Secretary of the Executive Council, as Temporary
Recorder.
Brother Weed then appointed the following committees by customary
rotation :

the following nominations for officers of this Convention :
President
LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01

Assistant Recorder David C. Peterson, Theta Theta '49
A motion was adopted that this report be unanimously accepted and the
Temporary Recorder be instructed to cast one ballot for the election of the
Permanent Officers nominated. The Temporary Recorder reported that the
ballot had been cast and the Permanent Officers had been elected.
President Weed introduced to the Convention the officers of the Fra
ternity and the members of the Executive Council who were present.
President Weed also introduced to the Convention various other alumni
including Harry E. Briggs, Epsilon, '03; R. H. Craig, Epsilon '12; Horace
R. Dougherty. Omega '96; Morris R. Holman. Theta Theta '23; C. S. F.
Lincoln. Kappa '91; and Jack J. Hensley, Theta Theta '11. As they were
introduced these Brothers each said a few words to the Convention. Certain
of these Brothers suggested that additional chapters of the Fraternity be
installed at appropriate colleges and universities. The suggestion was re
ferred to the Committee on New Business.
President Weed reported the formal calling of the Convention and
directed the attention of the delegates to the notice with respect to the time
and place of the Convention. An opportunity was afforded for a question
to be raised with respect to proper notice of the Convention, and the
Recorder was instructed to note that no question was raised as to failure
to receive due and proper notice of the Convention.
The Annual Communication of the Executive Council (See Appendix
A) was read by Robert I. Laggren, Xi '13.
On motion, duly adopted, this Communication was accepted and re
ferred to the Committee on Annual Communications. The Annual Com
munication included the names of Brothers whose deaths in the Armed
Services of this country and Canada had been officially reported during the
period since the last Convention.
President Weed requested the Recorder to call the roll of delegates,
and as this was done each delegate rose and was identified.
President Weed introduced to the Convention Charles H. Walker, Theta
Theta '17; C. H. Carlander, Theta Theta '17; John F. Reed, Pi '95; Roger
Caldwell, Phi '07; Ben Collard, Theta Theta '20; J. C. Bollinger, Theta
Theta '22; and Merville Mclnnis, Theta Theta '21. Each Brother so intro
duced rose and addressed the Convention briefly.
Upon motion, duly adopted, the Convention adjourned at 12:10 P.M.
to reconvene at 2 :00 P.M., Thursday, June 26, 1947.

Washington Athletic Club
Seattle. Washington

Theta�
^(Requested, and was granted, permission to yield temporarily
to the Theta Theta. the host Chapter).
Theta Theta�
(John Van Marshall, '46). During the past year the
Theta Theta has compiled a very strong record at the University of Wash
ington. The President of the student body of more than fifteen thousand
students is a member of the Chapter. The Chapter is the only organization
on the campus holding more than one seat on the Board of Control, which
is the top student governing body. The recent rushing program has been
very successful and active membership is in the vicinity of sixty men. The
Chapter has the best record in inter-mural sports participation on tht
campus. The financial position is good. The Chapter owns its own house
and has a strong reserve fund for new construction when prices are more
reasonable. "Down through the years, however, the Theta Theta has found
it increasingly difficult to maintain its position on the campus because of
the loss of prestige which we suffer in being separated by extreme distances
from other chapters of Psi Upsilon. Our strongest competitors are repre
sented in almost every region of the northwestern area from which we
draw most of our students. With the exception of our good friends at the
University of British Columbia, the nearest Psi U Chapter is at the Uni
versity of California, nine hundred miles away. In the conviction that
whatever enhances our position enhances that of the fraternity as a whole,
we of the Theta Theta are anxious for moderate expansion of Psi Upsilon
on the Pacific Coast. We are not willing to compromise the traditional
strength required of a chapter which successfully petitions Psi Upsilon,
and we are not interested in haphazard expansion, but we are convinced that
there are several colleges on the Pacific Coast in addition to California,
British Columbia and Washington, which could support strong Psi U
Chapters to the advantage of our fraternity."
[At the conclusion of the Theta Theta report a strong supporting
statement relative to moderate expansion on the Pacific Coast v/as made
by McDannell Brown, Theta Theta '23.]
Theta� (Robert C. Heidell, '48). The Chapter consists of thirty-eight
men and two pledges, and the majority of the actives are "G.I.'s". The
Chapter has maintained a prominent position on the campus, both in publi
cations and in sports. The Chapter House has been enlarged by an addition
to the dQrmitory section. Relations with the college and with other fra
ternities are, very good. The Chapter is desirous of informing the Conven
tion that- it. has taken a particularly strong position against anti-racial
feeling.. This stand has been very generally approved on the college campus.
.Strong; alumni support and an active program have co-operated to make
the record of the Chapter outstanding.
At the suggestion of the President, the program of oral reports from
the Chapters was interrupted to permit of the rendering of the annual
Treasurer's Report.

On motion, duly adopted, the Convention approved the transfer of the

(Clarence L. von Egloffstein, Delta '12) . The scholarship of
the Chapter is excellent. Among the top three of the seventeen fraternities
at N. Y. U. The Chapter House has been completely renovated and re
furnished. The Chapter is 100% ex-"G.I.'s". The alumni are enthusiastic
about the attitude and the record of the Chapter. Relations with the college
are now very cordial. The financial condition is excellent. The Chapter
believes expansion should be a matter of merit.
President Weed requested Benjamin T. Burton, Chi '21, Vice-President
of the Fraternity, to take the chair. This request was acceded to and the
Chapter reports were resumed.
Sigma�
(William E. McCool. Sigma '48). The Chapter is active on
th^ campus with forty-five members participating in all types of extra
curricular endeavors. Financially the Chapter is doing well, but there will
be appreciable future expenses for furniture and renovation. There is a
difference of opnion with the college as to the amount of rental assessed
against the_ Chapter. A strong freshman delegation bodes well for the
future. The Chapter has not done too well academically, but it is expected
that there will be a real improvement. The Chapter favors limited con
servative expansion.
Gamma� (J. R. Kingman, III. '49). Strong alumni support has
recently greatly aided the fraternities at Amherst, Gamma alumni took the
lead. The Chapter favors limited conservative expansion on the Pacific
Coast. The Chapter stands at the top on the Amherst campus.
Zeta� (William H. Spoor. '46). The Chapter hopes to entertain the
1949 Convention. It favors limited expansion on the Pacific Coast, but is
not in favor of entering the south. The Zeta stands well at Dartmouth in
all respects.
Lambda� (Walter S. Robinson. '19). The Chapter has ten active
members and one pledge. The Delta alumni and undergraduates have been
most helpful to the Lambda. The Chapter looks forward to resuming its
commanding position on the campus. The Chapter would prefer to limit
the expansion of the Fraternity to the mid-west and the Pacific Coast.
There would be strong objection to entering the south.
Kappa� (C. S. F. Lincoln. '91). There are seventy active members
of the Chapter. 90% of whom are "G.I.'s". A new Chapter House would
be desirable but. meanwhile, the present house has been renovated and

MINUTES OF THE MORNING SESSION
FRIDAY, JUNE 27. 1947
Washington Athletic Club
Seattle. Washington
The Convention was called to order by President Weed at 10:00 A.M.
On motion, duly adopted, the reading of the minutes of the preceding
session was dispensed with.
Oral reports from the Chapters were continued as follows :
Pi�
(F. R. W. Ross, Jr., '45). The Chapter requires a full year of
pledge training before initiation. There are sixty-eight Brothers and pledges
at present. Any Brother below a "C" average must study in the Chapter
House at least four nights a week. The Chapter uses its own pledge manual.
The Chapter rates well on the campus in all activities. It has four 'varsity
captains and the editor of the college magazine. The Chapter favors new
chapters except in the south. The Chapter favors the possibility of helping
any new chapter with a fund contributed to by the older chapters.
Chapter reports were interrupted to permit President Weed to appoint
the following Committee on Pledge Manual :
David K. Payne, Zeta Zeta '47, Chairman
Robert C. Heidell, Theta '46
Joseph K. Kingman, III, Gamma '49
Robert Mulligan, Phi '48
Preston Haglin, Mu '49
Richard R. Pegram, Epsilon '47
Edward T. Richards, Sigma '27
Oral reports from the Chapters were continued as follows :
Chi� (Fred L. Gault, '45). The Chapter is off to a very good start
and is maintaining a prominent position on the campus. Relationship
Iietween the college and the fraternities seems much better than before the
war. A very limited expansion is favored by the Chapter but emphasis
must continue to be placed on the quality of the petitioning group rather
than relying mainly on convenience of location.
Beta Beta� (Alexander M. Hunter, '48). Thirty-seven members and
three pledges constitute the present Chapter. The maximum number perPage Twelve

PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
mitted in the Chapter has been increased from forty to fifty. The members
actively and successfully participate in all academic, social and athletic
.endeavors. The Chapter finances are improving. Prospects for the future
are excellent. Relations with the other fraternities and with the college
are very good.
Eta�
(Frank Sturges, III, '48). The Eta had a very humble beginning
after the war, but the Chapter is now fully launched. The Chapter would
prefer deferred rushing instead of "cut-throat", but this is a matter on
which all fraternities must reach an agreement. The Chapter favors "lim
ited controlled" expansion in the west, the southwest or the midwest. The
Chapter future is bright and alumni help is a very decided factor.
Tau�
(John R. Herbert, '46). The House is in fairly good physical
shape, but the Chapter still has ideas and is after more funds. Alumni
have helped greatly, and the Chapter hopes for continued support. The
Chapter is not outstanding academically, but is very prominent in athletics
and publications. The membership favors a "limited expansion" at "well
accredited" schools. The Tau wishes to go on record as being anxious to
entertain the next Convention or. if that is not possible, to entertain the
Convention as soon as the Chapter would be in line for the honor.
Mu�
(Preston Haglin, '49). The problems of the Mu differ from
those of most of the other Chapters. The Mu started the past year with
sixty-four actives. It will probably have fifty actives next year. All mem
bers are "G.I.'s" so far. There is difficulty in filling the house dormitory
section, as most men live in Minneapolis or St. Paul. Expansion of a
limited nature is looked upon with favor. The Mu would be interested in
a connecting chapter link between the far west and the mid west.
Rho�
(John W. Sweeney, Jr.. '43). The House has been remodelled
and is in excellent shape. The alumni have been of great help and the
Chapter is very appreciative. The Chapter is not very prominent in intra
mural athletics but is represented on the 'varsity squads. Academically the
Chapter is doing very well and is quite near the top on the campus. Socially
the House is very active. The house-mother problem has come up again.
but has not been decided as yet.
Epsilon� (Richard R. Pegram, '47). The House reopened in the fall
of 1945 with seven members. Operating losses have been met by contribu
tions from alumni. The House is now back to a normal membership and
is financially sound. Relations with the college are very good. The Chapter
is definitely and actively interested in expansion in the west, particularly
in southern California. The alumni and undergraduates are planning for a
building fund in the near future, although it may be some time before
actual plans can be drawn.
Omicron�
(David J. Lamoree, '46). The House was returned in the
fall of 1946. Approximately $7,000.00 has been spent on redecorating.
There are thirty active members at present. Academically the Chapter rates

well in the upper half among the fraternities on the campus. It is well
represented in 'varsity sports and in intra-mural sports. Social events have
been very successful. The House is composed largely of "G.I's.". The
Chapter favors possible expansion in the west and southwest.
Delta Delta�
(Peter Ganyard, 'SO). The Chapter has been through
a difllicult but successful year. It started with only eight men, but is in
good shape now with fifty-one active members. The House has been re
decorated and considerable money has been spent on furnishings. The
Chapter favors conservative expansion, and thought of recommending that
a special list of prospective locations be drawn up for consideration- The
Chapter is prominent on the campus and enjoys friendly relations with the
college and all other fraternity groups.
Nu�
(Harold A. Logan, '46). Fraternities are not recognized by
Toronto University, and in many respects the Nu does not have problems
similar to those of other Chapters. There are no troubles or difficulties
whatsoever with the college, and relations are very friendly. There is an
informal interfraternity council, and all problems are handled in pleasant
and agreeable fashion. The Chapter now has about forty active members
and the future outlook is very bright. In scholarship and in athletics the
Chapter seems to be doing very well. Financially, the House is in the black
for the first time in several years. The alumni have been a great help.
A modest fund has been set aside for redecorating, and the Chapter hopes
to augment this amount. The Chapter wishes to suggest that a fraternity
tie be presented to each man on initiation. The Nu definitely favors expan
sion provided that the fraternity doesn't "go hog-wild". It is suggested
that other colleges in Canada might be seriously considered.
Epsilon Phi�
(Roy M. Liddy, '47). The Chapter favors expansion
and asks further consideration for Canada. The Chapter now has forty-two
members. Financially, it is doing very well, having reduced the mortgage
and provided funds for partial renovation. Relations with the alumni are
good. The Chapter stands very well on the campus, academically as well
as in sports and in social events. The past year has been very successful
in every way. Relations with the college are good. There have been some
attacks on fraternities by "Communists" but "we've had a lot of fun and we
got back at them."
Zeta Zeta� (David K. Payne, '47). In 1945 the Chapter had seven
Brothers. Now it has thirty-eight. Prospects are bright. The Chapter
and its alumni have made plans for a building fund and the project is well
launched. The undergraduates are active on the campus in all lines of
endeavor. The Chapter favors expansion on the West Coast between
Vancouver and San Francisco. It also favors locating another chapter
between Vancouver and Montreal.
Epsilon Nu� (Robert P. Gocke, '48). The Epsilon Nu has a large
membership�over sixty actives�but more than half are seniors. . The
Page Fourteen

PSI UPSILON FRAT E R N I T Y
Chapter House is in excellent shape. The Chapter has possibly been a bit
too active socially. At least, the college thought so. However, the Chapter
continues to stand well academically, and to be busy in campus activities.
A vigorous debate is anticipated on the house-mother question. The other
fraternities are with the Epsilon Nu on this matter, but the college is
forcing the issue. The Chapter favors limited expansion.
President Weed made certain announcements pertaining to the various
social occasions during the remainder of the day.
William C. Porter, Iota '49, Chairman of the Committee on Unfinished
Business, then reported to the Convention that there was no business pend
ing. On motion, duly passed, this report was accepted.
Alexander M. Hunter, Beta Beta '48. Chairman of the Committee on
New Business, read the report of that Committee recommending the adop
tion of the following resolutions :
1. Resolved: That the active chapters at this time prepare a list
of several colleges which have a new chapter potential; that once such
a list is prepared ind is approved by action of the Convention, the
Secretary of the Convention communicate with alumni and under
graduates of our present chapters who may reside near the afore
mentioned colleges, inviting them to investigate, as a committee,
opportunities, and to report back to the Council; and that, if such
reports indicate favoring circumstances, the active chapters be noti
fied and given the opportunity to send a representative, or to express
either approval or disapproval ; and that having been given the approval
of the active chapters, the local alumni committees, in each separate
instance, be given the authority to co-operate with the group in the
college and to prepare that group for petitioning Psi Upsilon. From
this point on the petition be handled in accordance with our constitu
tional methods.
2. Resolved: That the Executive Council be empowered to
designate a common and uniform Psi Upsilon tie.
3. Resolved: That the recommendation be given to the 1947 Con
vention that the 1948 Convention be held with the Tau Chapter at the
University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, at some date in
the spring designated by the Executive Council.
4. Resolved: That the Convention appreciates the untiring efforts
of the Executive Council and the officers of the Council on behalf of
the Chapters and the Fraternity as a whole.
5. Resolved: That the Convention appreciates the unselfish and
effective efforts of the Board of Governors of the Alumni Association
and its ofl&cers.
6. Resolved: That the Convention convey its thanks and appre
ciation to Edward C. Peattie, Phi '06, the Editor of the Diamond.
Page Fifteen

PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
7. Resolved: That the Recorder send letters of greeting to each
of the past Presidents of the Executive Council : Earl D. Babst, Iota
'93, Edward L. Stevens, Chi '99, and Scott Turner, Phi '02.
8. Resolved: That the Convention express its appreciation for his
work in presiding over all sessions of this Convention and for the able
manner in which he has conducted the meetings of the Executive
Council to LeRoy J. Weed, President of the Executive Council.
9. Resolved: That the delegates and members of the Psi Upsilon
Fraternity assembled in Convention in its 114th year as guests of the
Theta Theta Chapter. University of Washington. Seattle. Washington.
on June 26, 27 and 28, 1947. extend their hearty thanks to the Theta
Theta Chapter, its alumni and their committees for their cordial hospi
tality to the delegates and other members attending the Convention.
10. Resolved: That the Recorder be instructed to write a letter
to Dr. Raymond T. Allen, President of the University of Washington,
thanking him for his delightful and instructive address of welcome at
our Thursday morning meeting.
There was an immediate request for a discussion with reference to the
report of this committee. Numerous undergraduate and alumni Brothers
spoke in favor of or in opposition to the first resolution relative to the
matter of expansion of the Fraternity.
The discussion on the report was terminated by the President with the

seattle, washington
June 26. 27. and 28. 1947
The Executive Council cordially welcomes the delegates of our twentyeight Chapters and visiting members of the Fraternity to the 105th Conven
tion of Psi Upsilon, held in our 114th year.
We speak for all who are assembled here in extending warm thanks to
our hosts of the Theta Theta Chapter, undergraduates and alumni alike,
for their cordial hospitality and for their carefully laid and generous plans
for our entertainment.
During the war years, with most of the undergraduate Brothers in the
service of our country, the Conventions have necessarily been held under
the auspices of the Executive Council. A Convention has taken place each
year, with alumni Brothers acting as delegates for their Chapters, from
which it was impossible for undergraduates to be represented. The Council
now gladly relinquishes to the Theta Theta the duty as host and to the
Chapters their role as participants in a deliberative body.
Condition of Fraternity:
The condition of our Fraternity, after the rigorous war years, is such
as to justify optimism, but not inertia, since in some quarters the everpresent opposition to fraternities has not been relaxed.
All of our twenty-eight Chapters are operating. All Chapter houses
have been re-opened. The total undergraduate membership of the Frater
nity is upwards of 1,134, a figure which contrasts interestingly with last
year's total of 437, and that of 1945, 253. The normal undergraduate mem
bership in pre-war years was about 875.
Almost all of the Chapters are engaged in renovating their Houses or
in raising funds for that purpose. Some renovations have been completed.
The Zeta Zeta, which has hitherto occupied rented premises, is conducting
a campaign for funds with a view to purchasing or building their own
House. The Lambda Chapter has re-opened with a small group of under
graduates, and has resumed its former quarters in one of the Columbia
University dormitories.
Page Twenty-three

RECORDS OF THE CONVENTION
A spirit of interest, enthusiasm and loyalty to the Fraternity, its tra
ditions and ideals, has been noticeable to members of the Council when
making their Chapter visitations. This is an even more hopeful sign than
the increased (perhaps somewhat inflated) membership.
The Executive Council:
The Executive Council has held six meetings during the year. That
on September 9 antedated the Convention held in Chicago on September 16
and 17. The five subsequent meetings were held on October 8, November
25, February 3, April 1, and May 5. On February 3, the members of the
Board of Governors of the Alumni Association attended the meeting of
the Council, and the members of the Council were guests at the Board of
Governors meeting which was held on the same occasion.
At the meeting on October 8, Brother Scott Turner. Phi '02. who had
faithfully served as President of the Executive Council for over nine years.
including the difficult war years, resigned his office. Brother LeRoy J.
Weed, Theta '01, was elected President. Brother Weed has served on the
Council since 1928. Under his presidency, the Council hopes successfully to
continue its service to the Fraternity.
The terms of the following members expire on this occasion : Herbert
J. Flagg, George C. Kingsley, and Samuel L. Rosenberry. It is therefore
incumbent on this Convention to elect three Brothers to the Executive
Council, each for the term of five years.
For the benefit of the younger Brothers who are not familiar with the
organization of Psi Upsilon, let us once more call to your attention the
aims and functions of the Executive Council :
The members of the Executive Council are elected by the Convention.
They serve without compensation and pay their own expenses in making
Chapter visits. Membership on the Council demands a willingness to serve
the Fraternity without emoluments of any kind beyond that of a knowl
edge of a service well done.
It is essential that members of Council be able to attend the five or
six meetings a year without undue sacrifice either of time or of money.
Ordinarily, it is not feasible to elect to membership on the Council indi
viduals who are so geographically located that attendance at Council meet
ings would be unduly burdensome. In the past, some Conventions have
enthusiastically endorsed for membership individuals who could not pos
sibly contribute to the very real work and effort required of members of
Council. It is to be hoped that selections of this sort will not be frequent
and that the Conventions will elect alumni representatives who are located
within comparatively easy traveling distance of New York City, and whose
business affairs will permit of the expenditure of a reasonable amount of
time and effort on behalf of the Fraternity.
1948 Convention :
This Convention with the Theta Theta has the duty of arranging for
Twenty-four

RECORDS OF THE CONVENTION
the holding of the 1948 Convention. The Fraternity has had an outstanding
record insofar as Conventions are concerned. During the Civil War the
Convention of 1862 was unable to transact business because no quorum was
present, and during World War I no Convention was held in 1917. With
these exceptions, the Conventions have been uninterrupted. The Fraternity
and its Executive Council can take pride in the continuance of the Con
ventions without interruption throughout the period of World War II.
This year we return to our normal procedure of holding the Conven
tions with Chapters in rotation. This is the first time that the Theta Theta
has acted as host. The three latest additions to our Chapter Roll, the
Epsilon Phi, the Zeta Zeta, and the Epsilon Nu, have not as yet entertained
our annual sessions. In the ordinary rotation, the Chapters next in line for
the Convention are the Epsilon, which held the Convention in 1915; Zeta,
1916; Mu, 1919; Tau, 1920; Xi. 1921; and Rho, 1923. Inasmuch as this
Convention is being held on the Pacific Coast, and inasmuch as the Convenof 1946 was held in Chicago, it would seem advisable that the 1948 Con
vention should be held in New England or the middle Atlantic States.
The Diamond :
Because of the continued paper shortage and increased costs of produc
tion, it has been necessary to hold The Diamond, with the exception of one
issue, to its wartime size of thirty-two pages. It has been possible, how
ever, somewhat to improve the appearance of the magazine by using a better
quality of paper, not previously available, and by increasing the number of
cuts per issue.
It is hoped next year gradually to expand and improve the magazine
until it reaches its pre-war size and physical appearance.
In quality of content, every effort has been made to maintain our usual
standards, although the amount of news and other material published has
necessarily been limited by the diminished number of pages.
The Editor of The Diamond performs a labor of love. The Fraternity
has been fortunate in being able to secure intelligent, devoted Brothers to
serve as editors and perform such services without compensation. Brother
Edward C. Peattie. Phi '06, has continued his fine work as Editor and he
deserves the thanks of this Convention and the Fraternity.
Pledge Manual :
Brother Edward T. Richards, the Secretary of the Council, has in the
course of preparation a new Pledge Manual which will be supplied to the
Chapters for distribution among the pledgees. In this connection, it is
desired that this Convention adopt a uniform code of procedure in offering
a pledge to any undergraduate.
Scholarship :
The reports received this year on the scholarship of our Chapters have
not been comprehensive, so that it is impossible to arrive at any general
conclusion. However, it may be well to remind our Chapters that one of
Twenty-five

RECORDS OF THE CONVENTION
the main grounds for attacks on the fraternity system is based on the
alleged low scholarship standards of the fraternities. Due to the G.I. Bill
of Rights, standards of admission are probably higher than heretofore.
The inability of colleges to accept many of those who apply for admission
has automatically compelled a higher standard of admission requirements.
It is incumbent upon each Chapter of this Fraternity to see that the
scholastic standard of its members is jealously carried on. If the frater
nity system shall survive, the scholarship of Fraternity members must be
superior to that of the general student body.
Expansion :
The policy to be followed in regard to expansion of the Fraternity
through the installation of additional chapters has been discussed by vari
ous alumni associations and by the Executive Council. During the 114
years of its existence, Psi Upsilon has always been a conservative frater
nity. The question has been raised, in view of the many changing condi
tions relative to college life, if it might not be advisable to reverse this
policy and stimulate local groups in various selected colleges to apply to
Psi Upsilon for the establishment of chapters. The further question has
been raised as to whether Psi Upsilon ought not to expand more rapidly on
the Pacific Coast, and ought not to consider seriously the installation of
Chapters at selected colleges and universities in the southwestern and
southern section of our country.
Whatever policy may be adopted, it is important that the subject receive
the most careful discussion.

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL OF PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
Report of the Treasurer
1947
There is presented herewith a statement of the net worth of the various
funds of the Fraternity held by the Executive Council as of April 30,
1947, a summary of income and expenses of the various funds for the year
ended April 30, 1947. and certain comparative figures for the year ended
April 30. 1946. A list of investments held in the General Fund, the Bridg
man Fund, the Douglas Fund and the Diamond Life Subscription Fund
is also set forth.
The net worth of the various funds increased $5,823 during the year,
after transferring the total amount received for Diamond Life subscrip
tions, viz., $9,585, to the Reserve for Diamond Life Subscriptions. That we
were able to show a $5,823 increase in net assets was in part due to for
tuitous security profits amounting to $3,873. We were able to operate
throughout the war without dipping into our reserve funds because of
security profits, but we can not count on these as a regular occurrence and
so your Treasurer is happy to report that with the opening of all the
chapters and with the return of the undergraduates to the colleges our
normal sources of revenue, composed largely of undergraduate dues and
income from investments, exceeded our expenses by $1,950 in the past year.
This figure arises out of an excess of income over expenses (without
counting security profits) of $1,348 in the General Fund, $446 in the
Diamond Life Subscription Fund and $1,398 in the Convention Fund, and
a loss of $1,242 in the Diamond Fund for the publishing ot the Diamond.
This loss is to be taken care of by transferring $1,250 to the Diamond
Fund from the General Fund, which will still leave a surplus for the year
of $1,735 in the General Fund. This Convention is asked to authorize this
transfer.
These figures all indicate that the various funds are in good shape
except in respect to meeting the costs of publishing The Diamond. The
Diamond Committee wish to improve the quality of The Diamond and also
to increase its size. Paper and printing costs have been increasing. This
creates a problem which is being studied, and the suggestion has been made
that it may be necessary to raise the price of life subscriptions. Your
Treasurer, however, believes that every effort should be made to avoid
any such increase in the price of the life subscriptions and that Diamond
deficits should be met from the surplus of other funds until such time as
the income from the Diamond Life Subscription Reserve Fund can be
built up to a figure which will meet Diamond publishing costs. The rea
son for the Diamond deficits is that for years all life subscription moneys
were spent as received and nothing was accumulated as a reserve to meet

the liability of furnishing copies of The Diamond to life subscribers.
However eight years ago the policy of funding Diamond life subscription

The statement shows that as of April 30. 1947 gross accounts receiva

An inspection of our list of investments indicates that we are in a

$1,000.
The Treasurer takes this opportunity to remind the Brothers that every

year.
The Treasurer sincerely thanks the Chapter Treasurers for their co
